tagline: A freshwater spring feeds a short river beside the Missouri.
intro: Giant Springs Road reaches Giant Springs State Park just outside Great Falls. The park encompasses nearly 14 miles of Missouri River shoreline. Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks describes a landscape of freshwater springs, river waterfalls and trails, with a fish hatchery beside the spring water.

The Lewis and Clark Expedition recorded the springs in 1805. The nearby falls forced the expedition into a portage that took nearly a month. In 1998, the Lewis and Clark Interpretive Center opened above the Missouri, with exhibits on the expedition’s portage.

At the interpretive center, the river lies below a cliff. At Giant Springs, water emerges on the Missouri’s east bank, downstream of Great Falls. The Roe River carries it into the Missouri, completing a journey only 201 feet long at its longest constant point.

moments.title: Lewis and Clark Interpretive Center
moments.text: The Lewis and Clark Interpretive Center occupies a cliff above the Missouri near Crooked Falls. The Forest Service opened it in 1998 to tell the story of the expedition’s passage through central Montana. That passage included a portage around the Great Falls that took nearly a month. Exhibits address both the portage and the Native peoples of the area. The center includes an exhibit hall, a theater, a store and classrooms. The center’s position above the Missouri connects the expedition’s overland detour with the waterway that made the long portage necessary.

moments.title: Giant Springs
moments.text: Giant Springs begins with snowmelt in the Little Belt Mountains, 60 miles away. The water travels through Madison Limestone before emerging at a constant 54 degrees Fahrenheit. The spring produces over 156 million gallons each day. Some of that water supplies a state trout hatchery that raises mostly rainbow trout. The spring is the central feature of Giant Springs State Park, where the hatchery has a visitor center and a show pond. Beneath the park’s recreational setting is a water system connecting distant mountains with the Missouri’s bank.
moments.notice: Spring water cascades into the Roe River.

moments.title: Roe River
moments.text: The Roe River links Giant Springs with the Missouri in 201 feet at its longest constant point. Its name came before its record. In 1987, Susie Nardlinger’s fifth-grade students at Lincoln Elementary School began a campaign to have it recognized as the world’s shortest river. First they petitioned the United States Board on Geographic Names to accept Roe River for the unnamed stream. Then they submitted their proposal to Guinness, which awarded the title in 1989. Guinness dropped the category in 2006; the river’s short passage from spring to Missouri remains its defining feature.
